slides.0.title: Serving temperature, decanting and glassware
slides.0.subtitle: Temperature and time can make one bottle taste like two
slides.1.title: Serving temperatures
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Well chilled (about 6–10°C)
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Sparkling and sweet wines: low temperatures keep the mousse fine and sweet wines fresh
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Chilled (about 7–13°C)
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Light whites and rosés colder (about 7–10°C), full or oaked whites a little warmer (about 10–13°C); too cold masks aroma and texture
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Reds (about 13–18°C)
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Light reds can be lightly chilled (about 13°C), medium to full reds about 15–18°C; “room temperature” in a warm restaurant is often too high and makes alcohol stand out
slides.1.content: Too cold hides aroma, too warm exaggerates alcohol: serving temperature is a balance between the two.
slides.2.title: Decanting and glassware
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Decanting purpose 1: removing sediment
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Old reds and Vintage Port often throw sediment; stand the bottle upright beforehand, pour in front of a light and stop when the sediment reaches the neck
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Decanting purpose 2: aeration
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Young, structured reds (and some whites) open up and lose reductive notes with air; very old wines need care, as too much air can make fragile aromas fade
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Glassware and storage
slides.2.highlights.2.content: A generous bowl that narrows slightly at the rim concentrates aroma; glasses must be clean and free of detergent smell. Ideal cellar: a steady 12–14°C, moderate humidity, darkness, no vibration, bottles lying down to keep corks moist
slides.2.content: Decide why to decant before deciding whether, and for how long.
slides.3.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What is roughly the serving temperature for medium to full-bodied reds?
Warm restaurant rooms are often too hot.
What is the main purpose of decanting an old red?
Too much air can even make old wine lose aroma.
Why do young, structured reds benefit from decanting?
B. Air opens the aromas and dispels reduction
What is roughly the ideal cellar temperature?
Stability matters more than the exact figure.
